newsitem.title: JAPAN: Atomic firm spotlights reform-proof Japan agencies.
newsitem.headline: Atomic firm spotlights reform-proof Japan agencies.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto began the year vowing to "go down in flames" if he failed to trim state spending and bloated bureaucracies under a reform scheme in which no government body would be sacrosanct.

However, if the state-run Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC) is typical, Hashimoto looks like he will be able to do little more than smoulder in anger as his reforms get trampled in a vast herd of sacred cows.

The PNC, involved in three nuclear scandals in 18 months, thrived for decades in an atmosphere in which its mission -- pursuing energy self-sufficiency with homegrown technology -- was held to be more important than questions of accountability or safety, nuclear power critics say.
But the state-run nuclear research firm is merely the most dangerous of dozens of the 800-lb godzillas the frustrated Hashimoto must tackle in the fight to carry out ambitious administrative reforms.

And unlike the clumsy PNC, which was not even on the chopping block until the recent fiascoes, many of those bodies are well prepared to deftly dodge Hashimoto's reforms with help from members of his own political party.
A furious Hashimoto this week declared the PNC "completely hopeless" after he learned it had waited 30 hours before reporting a radiation leak at a power plant in western Japan.

That remark came less than a week after the PNC's admission that it bungled the handling of a fire and explosion last month at a nuclear fuel reprocessing plant. It then later admitted it lied in its official report.
"I am so angry I cannot utter a single word," Hashimoto said.

One day later, the Science and Technology Agency, the cabinet-level body which oversees nuclear research and founded the PNC, took the unprecedented step of filing a legal complaint against its prodigal son.

If the PNC's admitted deception and apparent incompetence in the nuclear accidents riveted Japan's attention because of the lethal nature of radiation, many state institutions have similar problems, said a former Hashimoto cabinet minister.

Recent examples have included health officials who allowed the distribution of HIV-tainted blood long after the dangers were known, and farm officials and lobbyists who shielded agricultural financial institutions from responsibility for billions of dollars of reckless real estate lending.

The common denominator of these problems is a resistance to accountability and reform bred by cozy ties between bureaucrats and politicians in Hashimoto's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), the ex-minister said.

On Thursday, the opening day of ministerial hearings on the reform scheme, Japanese newspapers catalogued comments by officials who said "they agreed in principle" with the reform goals but opposed specific plans proposed for their ministries.
The prime minister's programme features a halving of central government ministries, a culling of budget-busting state-run firms and a "Big Bang" shake-up of the country's financial sector.

The scheme has been held out as a cure for Japanese ills ranging from huge public sector deficits to stagnant stock markets. The mere promise of reform has at least temporarily staved off trade friction with the United States.

Many Japanese observers, however, have raised concerns that the reforms will be debated to death in committees packed with officials, politicians and industry figures with an interest in blocking change.
"We see no sign whatsoever of procedures or strategy, only a debate that is dissipating," the conservative daily newspaper Sankei Shimbun said in an editorial.
The editorial said Hashimoto lacked a grand vision to unify reforms and was "tossing the ball to myriad, disconnected deliberation councils".

If Hashimoto fails, he will join the long line of modern Japanese prime ministers who delivered less than they promised because their schemes were gutted by bureaucrats and by politicians who depend on ministries for hometown pork-barrel spending.
